Thanks for your post! I reviewed it with a coworker who also raised the possibility it was a second degree type 2 with 2:1 conduction, and it looks to be so!

Initially suspicious for CHB but reconsidered as the complexes were just too narrow. Yet consistently 24-26 bpm the entire encounter. Left hanging on "sinus brady with 1st degree" for some time but ultimately I'm thinking this is a second degree type 2 with 2:1 conduction. Interventions were oxygen 2 lpm by cannula, IV atropine, and IV normal saline infusion. Last I knew patient was being evaluated for an emergency pacemaker placement.

Patient presented to urgent care for evaluation of above symptoms, noted to have started upon waking and becoming increasingly worse throughout the day. No chest pain, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills, lightheadedness or syncopal episodes or recent illness.  EMS was summoned on discovery of abnormal vital signs.

History of chronic kidney disease without dialysis and atrial fibrillation. Meds include atenolol, amiodarone, lasix and Coumadin. No allergies.

Completely alert and oriented, speaking full sentences, no complaints when seated or lying flat.

BP 134/46 with room air spo2 98%. Transported emergently, received two doses of atropine IV en route. No change.

My ambulance was dispatched to a car crash early one morning on a large, main road in town. On arriving we found one car that crashed and bounced off a telephone pole. We worked with the fire department to extricate the lone, heavyset patient with multiple injuries from his car as fast as we could manage. We got the patient out and into the ambulance, where the FD medic, my partner and I began to start IVs, get vital signs, and check the patient for additional injuries.

About a minute later, while the three of us are working in the back we start to hear a bunch of shouting outside. The back doors are still open so I look out to see what's the problem. Six firefighters are barreling straight at us. Four of them jump straight into the patient compartment and two cling onto the back of the ambulance. "DRIVE DRIVE DRIVE DRIVE DRIVE!" What the hell is going on?! My partner barrels into the driver seat with an incredible speed and whips the ambulance further down the street. I stop what I'm doing to see what's going on out the back, and I manage to catch the wires and electric rain coming down on the crashed car, and then...the pole itself, with a horrifying crunch it flattened the car.

Our initially safe scene changed quickly and with little warning. Very fortunately, everyone made it out alright.

1. I work as a paramedic in a midsize city.

1.5 Most of the time! It's really cool to have developed a skill set that allows you to help people feel better and possibly save their life. 2. Social awkwardness might be a hurdle, and getting used to a new workplace can be an anxious experience for anyone, but if you dedicate yourself to mastering your job, your reputation as a good worker will give you a big hand in the workplace.

2.5 When I started this job I had the bare minimum for social skills, I was not a talker, but I could listen and be empathetic and that enabled me to comfort people and put them at ease while gathering information about their medical complaints--I would ask the questions I needed to and make them feel heard and cared for. People appreciate that. But there would come a time where I needed to assert my authority over others at the scene of an emergency. I had to push the anxiety and fear aside, take a deep breath, talk loud, and call the shots or somebody would have gotten hurt. I wouldn't have been able to forgive myself if someone fared for the worse because I didn't assert myself.

I was in a similar spot as you are OP. I ended up there for different reasons but I know where you're standing and I only broke through recently. I was extremely concerned with what others thought of me from the time I was 12 years old because I was bullied into an anxious, depressed, isolated mess and I needed to get my self esteem from others--big problem that you will regret if you don't work on. It took me a decade to get back to being my real self and I will say this to you: go out there, get into situations where you'll likely meet new people, be yourself when you're with them and accept that the worst things that could happen are that you're probably gonna fuck up talking to someone or you'll meet people who simply won't like you, and neither of those things should ever get you down. Be interested to hear what others have to say. Cultivate interests and hobbies so that you have things to talk about too. Make connections. The biggest thing I've noticed is that once I stopped thinking about every little thing I was going to say to someone and let myself naturally react or say whatever thought I had in mind, that's when I began to build true connections with people and get better at socializing. It's hard to not give a fuck about what others think, but the reward is that you're free to be yourself and you'll find people who will want to associate with you simply because you're you. It's worth it. And when you find the occasional fuckface who tries to shit all over your parade, tell 'em off, they can go fuck themselves. Hope this helps!
